title: A variable-capacitance vibration-to-electric energy harvester
venue: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I Fundamental Theory and Applications

sections.heading: A Variable-Capacitance Vibration-to-ElectricEnergy Harvester
sections.text:
Bernard C. Yen, Student Member, IEEE, and Jeffrey H. Lang, Fellow, IEEE

Abstract—Past research on vibration energy harvesting has focused primarily on the use of magnets or piezoelectric materials as the basis of energy transduction, with few experimental studies implementing variable-capacitance-based scavenging. In contrast, this paper presents the design and demonstration of a variable-capacitance vibration energy harvester that combines an asynchronous diode-based charge pump with an inductive energy flyback circuit to deliver $1 . 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { { W } }$ to a resistive load. A cantilever beam variable capacitor with a 650-pF dc capacitance and a 348-pF zero-to-peak ac capacitance, formed by a $\mathbf { 4 3 . 5 6 \ c m ^ { 2 } }$ spring steel top plate attached to an aluminum base, drives the charge pump at its out-of-plane resonant frequency of $\mathbf { 1 . 5 6 \ k H z }$ The entire harvester requires only one gated MOSFET for energy flyback control, greatly simplifying the clocking scheme and avoiding synchronization issues. Furthermore, the system exhibits a startup voltage requirement below $\mathbf { 8 9 } \mathbf { m V } ,$ indicating that it can potentially be turned on using just a piezoelectric film.

Index Terms—Variable-capacitance-based energy conversion, vibration energy harvesting, vibration energy scavenging.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
N RESPONSE TO a growing interest in autonomous systems, such as RF sensor nodes that must operate for prolonged periods of time without human intervention, vibration-to-electric energy harvesters have attracted wide research interest. Three main strategies for energy transduction dominate: piezoelectric, magnetic, and electric. Magnetic harvesting can be further categorized into systems with a time-varying inductor and systems that employ moving permanent magnets. Likewise, electric harvesting employs either a time-varying capacitor or a moving permanent electret.

Piezoelectric materials, such as quartz and barium titanate, contain permanently polarized structures that produce an electric field when the materials deform due to imposed mechanical forces [1]. Such a mechanically excited element can be modeled as a current source with a capacitive source impedance [2] where the current amplitude depends on the applied force. Therefore, if the material is connected to a vibration source, it can harvest the vibration energy and generate electric power [3], [4].

Magnetic energy harvesters, on the other hand, convert vibration energy into an induced voltage across wire coils, which can then deliver power to a load. This is typically done by attaching either a permanent magnet, such as that made from Neodymium

Iron Boron, or a coil of wire onto a cantilever beam that is vibrationally actuated; the other element remains fixed [5], [6]. In either scenario, the coil will cut through magnetic flux as the cantilever beam vibrates, creating an induced voltage at the terminals of the coil. Vibration energy can also be transduced using a variable inductor, although no such studies have been reported to date, presumably due to the inherent advantages of permanent magnets.

Finally, electric energy harvesting transduces vibration energy through the electric fields between a parallel plate capacitor. Typically, charge is injected into the capacitor at maximum capacitance and pulled off at minimum capacitance. Between these points, vibration separates the plates against their attractive force, performing work on the injected charge, which is then harvested [7]–[10]. Besides the variable capacitor, one can also employ a moving layer of permanently embedded charge, or electret, to carry out electric energy harvesting [11], although such systems currently have power densities inferior to those using variable capacitors.

Roundy et al. prototyped a simple variable-capacitance-based charge pump and showed that mechanical-to-electrical energy transduction was possible, but they did not explore the regime where the harvester saturates due to the lack of an energy flyback path [12]. Mur-Miranda conducted extensive studies on a synchronously excited capacitive energy harvester involving two active switches [8]. Although energy conversion was demonstrated, difficulties in gate clocking and inefficiencies of the power electronics prevented net energy conversion to a load. Miyazaki et al. improved the timing scheme of this topology and achieved $1 2 0 ~ \mathrm { n W }$ of converted power from a $4 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ vibration [9]. However, they did not analyze whether energy injection from the clock signal contributed to the harvested energy. As this paper will show, such energy injection can be significant, and can be mistaken for converted energy. Here, we present an optimized asynchronous capacitive energy harvester that requires only one active switch, thereby greatly simplifying clocking. For this paper, emphasis is placed on the circuitry, not on the implementation of the variable capacitor. The circuit employs a charge pump in its forward harvesting path and an inductive energy flyback to return net energy to a central reservoir. The harvester is demonstrated experimentally using a spring steel variable capacitor with capacitance variation between $3 0 2 \ \mathrm { p F }$ and $9 9 8 \ \mathrm { p F }$ and an out-of-plane resonant frequency of $1 . 5 6 \mathrm { k H z }$ . It delivers $1 . 8 – \mu \mathsf { W }$ of power to a resistive load, translating to an efficiency of $1 9 . 1 \%$ . Experimental data prove that net energy conversion does not result from clock energy injection.

Buck-converter flyback is presented here as a high-efficiency standard baseline implementation against which other schemes, such as switched-capacitor flyback, can be compared. Thus, even though the flyback circuitry involves an inductor, it is worthwhile examining. When employed as part of an integrated system, the required inductor in the flyback path could be implemented as an external component. Alternatively, planar inductors could be deposited or electroplated as part of the fabrication process [13].

sections.heading: II. POWER ELECTRONICS
sections.text:
Fig. 1 shows a block diagram of the capacitor-based energy harvester. The charge pump in the forward path transduces vibration energy into electric energy, which is then delivered to a temporary storage. Periodically, the inductive flyback circuit sends the harvested energy back to a reservoir that powers the attached load, priming the charge pump. A circuit implementation of the block diagram is shown in Fig. 2, with $R _ { \mathrm { L O A D } }$ representing the load. The charge pump consists of two diodes, $D _ { 1 }$ and $D _ { 2 }$ , that sandwich a variable capacitor $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ . The flyback section includes a gated MOSFET, freewheeling diode $D _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ , and inductor $L _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } ; \ R _ { \mathrm { W I R E } }$ and $R _ { \mathrm { C O R E } }$ model the winding and core loss of the inductor, respectively. Finally, the reservoir $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ and temporary storage $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ are each formed by a single capacitor under the requirement that $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } } \gg C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ .

In this paper, the MOSFET gate drive is powered from an external power supply for simplicity. It is recognized that the gate drive, along with other required control logic, must ultimately be powered directly from the harvested energy. This appears to be feasible for an integrated system because power generation on the order of microwatts is demonstrated below. Based on a typical MOSFET gate-source capacitance of $C _ { \mathrm { G S } } = 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { p F } .$ a drive voltage of $v _ { \mathrm { G S } } = 1 \mathrm { v }$ for an IC implementation, and a drive frequency of $f _ { \mathrm { C L K } } = 4 7 5 \mathrm { \ : H z }$ , the power dissipated in driving the MOSFET gate is

$$
P _ { \mathrm { C L K } } = C _ { \mathrm { G S } } v _ { \mathrm { G S } } ^ { 2 } f _ { \mathrm { C L K } } = 5 0 \mathrm { n W } .
$$

Thus, the harvested energy should be adequate.

sections.heading: A. Charge Pump Section
sections.text:
To understand the transduction of vibration energy to electric energy, assume initially that $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } } ~ = ~ v _ { \mathrm { R E S } } ~ = ~ v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ and $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } } ~ { = } ~ C _ { \mathrm { M A X } }$ , the maximum capacitance of the variable capacitor. At this point, both $D _ { 1 }$ and $D _ { 2 }$ are off, meaning that $Q _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ , the charge on the variable capacitor, cannot change. As ambient vibration pulls the capacitor plates apart, $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ decreases, which causes $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ to rise given constant $Q _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ . This voltage rise eventually turns on $D _ { 2 }$ , resulting in the partial discharge of $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ into $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ with $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } } = v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ . When the vibration reverses direction, $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ increases, causing $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ to drop, thereby turning off $D _ { 2 }$ . As $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ drops further, $D _ { 1 }$ turns on, which results in charge injection from $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ to $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ . This charging causes $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ to be held at $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ . The cycle repeats itself as charge and energy are pumped into $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ . Without the flyback section, will eventually saturate. Because this saturation voltage impacts the overall energy harvester performance, it is now computed analytically. Let the variable capacitor exhibit $C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } \leq C _ { \mathrm { V A R } } \leq C _ { \mathrm { M A X } }$ , and define a complete energy harvesting cycle as one variation of $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ from $C _ { \mathrm { M A X } }$ to $C _ { \mathrm { M I N } }$ and back to $C _ { \mathrm { M A X } }$ . Let $\scriptstyle v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , n }$ , where $n$ is an integer index starting from 0, represent the voltage on $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ at the end of $n$ cycles. Based on this definition, $\mathcal { V } _ { \mathrm { S T O R E , 0 } } ~ = ~ \mathcal { V } _ { \mathrm { R E S } } .$ . Furthermore, since $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } } \gg C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } .$ approximate $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ as a constant voltage source. Finally, assume the diodes are ideal. ![](images/90b1761f311d2094014ee6bdea0ba96e0622ffa0b307bd6a456ebdf275b8cf48.jpg) Fig. 3. Equivalent circuit diagrams for different parts of the harvesting cycle. (a) Start of first half of cycle (b) Start of second half of cycle. ![](images/86250ebd61b436d3fc6c71868020ed83264d25f04acaefaec75d7c7e7f3abf5f.jpg) Fig. 4. $Q - V$ plane contour representing one energy harvesting cycle. Fig. 3(a) shows an equivalent circuit diagram at the start of cycle $n$ . At this point, the total charge, $Q _ { \mathrm { T O T A L } }$ , stored in $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ and $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ is $$ Q _ { \mathrm { T O T A L } , n - 1 } = C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } + C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , n - 1 } . $$ Next, as $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ decreases, $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ rises so that $D _ { 1 }$ immediately turns off and $Q _ { \mathrm { T O T A L } }$ remains constant. Eventually, $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ increases enough so that $D _ { 2 }$ turns on and the equivalent circuit diagram shown in Fig. 3(b) results. During this part of the cycle, charge is transferred from $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ to $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ , giving $$ \begin{array}{c} v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } = \frac { C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } } { C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } + C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } } v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , n - 1 } \\ { + \frac { C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } } { C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } + C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } } V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } } \end{array} $$ at the end of the half cycle. Then, as $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ increases and $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ decreases, $D _ { 2 }$ immediately turns off, keeping the charge on $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ , and hence , constant throughout the remainder of the cycle. Therefore, $$ v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , n } = v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } $$ where $v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ is taken from (3). Because charge is transferred from $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ to $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ during the cycle, $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ will head toward a voltage that is less than $V _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ as $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ continues to increase. Therefore, $D _ { 1 }$ is guaranteed to turn on by the point when $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } } = C _ { \mathrm { M A X } }$ , so Fig. 3(a) is again the equivalent circuit diagram for the charge pump at the start of the next cycle. Define $$ \begin{array} { r l } & { \alpha { = } \frac { C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } } { C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } + C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } } } \\ & { \beta { = } \frac { C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } } { C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } + C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } } V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } } \end{array} $$ so that (3) and (4) can be rewritten as $$ v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , n } = \alpha v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , n - 1 } + \beta $$ which is a recurrence relation in the variable $\scriptstyle v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , i }$ . From [14], the solution of this recurrence relation is $$ \begin{array} { r l } { { \boldsymbol { v } _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , n } = V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } [ ( 1 - \frac { C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } } { C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } } ) } \quad } & { } \\ & { \qquad \times ( \frac { C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } } { C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } + C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } } ) ^ { n } + \frac { C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } } { C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } } ] . } \end{array} $$ To determine the saturation value of $v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ without energy flyback, substitute $n = \infty$ to obtain $$ v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E , \infty } } = \frac { C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } } { C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } } V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } . $$ Equation (9) indicates that the saturation value is related to the ratio $C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } / C _ { \mathrm { M I N } }$ . This equation may be rewritten as $$ v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E , infty } } = \frac { C _ { \mathrm { D C } } + C _ { \mathrm { A C } } } { C _ { \mathrm { D C } } - C _ { \mathrm { A C } } } V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } $$ where $C _ { \mathrm { D C } }$ represents the average value of $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ and $C _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ represents its zero-to-peak capacitance variation. From (10), it is apparent that DC parasitic capacitances in parallel with $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ must be minimized to prevent early saturation. The energy transduction process just described can also be viewed graphically as a $Q - V$ plane contour shown in Fig. 4. In this diagram, Point 1 corresponds to the moment when both $D _ { 1 }$ and $D _ { 2 }$ are off and the capacitor plates are just starting to pull apart for the $n$ th energy conversion cycle. At Point 2, $D _ { 1 }$ turns on, allowing charge to transfer from $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ to $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ ; correspondingly $Q _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ falls from Point 2 to Point 3. During this part of the cycle, $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } } = v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ . At Point 3, vibration has pulled the capacitor plates to their maximum separation, decreasing $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ to $C _ { \mathrm { M I N } }$ . Next, $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ increases and $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ falls, turning off $D _ { 2 }$ . Correspondingly, $Q _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ remains constant until Point 4, at which time $D _ { 1 }$ turns on and $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ is held at $V _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ . (b) Charge leakage. The area within the closed curve in Fig. 4 equals the mechanical vibration energy converted to electrical energy and delivered to $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ . As the cycles advance, Point 2 moves to the right and Point 3 rises to meet it. At the same time, Point 4 rises to meet Point 1, and the converted energy shrinks to zero as $\scriptstyle v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , n }$ saturates. Because of this, it is important to send the energy stored in $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ back to $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ quickly enough to permit continuous energy conversion. This is the purpose of the flyback circuitry shown in Figs. 1 and 2.

sections.heading: B. Inductive Flyback Section
sections.text:
To power the attached load and prevent from saturating, an inductive flyback circuit, modeled after a DC/DC buck converter and shown in Fig. 2, complements the charge pump. Nominally in its off state, the MOSFET switch turns on every few energy harvesting cycles to energize $\boldsymbol { L } _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ . The current $i _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ ramps up according to

$$
\frac { d i _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } } { d t } = \frac { v _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } } { L _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } }
$$

where $v _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } = v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } - v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ . After $D T _ { \mathrm { C L K } }$ , where $D$ represents the clock duty ratio and $T _ { \mathrm { C L K } }$ represents the clock period, the MOSFET turns off, forcing $i _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ to commutate to the freewheeling diode $D _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ . This makes $v _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } = - v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ , so

$$
\frac { d i _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } } { d t } = - \frac { v _ { \mathrm { R E S } } } { L _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } }
$$

until $i _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } = 0 \mathrm { A }$ , at which point the diode turns off. In this way, energy is transferred from $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ back to $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ where it can power the load, represented here by $R _ { \mathrm { L O A D } }$ . Note that it is not necessary for this process to be synchronized with the energy conversion cycles described in Section II-A. Indeed, it might be best to initiate the energy flyback whenever rises to a threshold value. This simplifies the control of the MOSFET switch by making it independent of the motion of the variable capacitor.

sections.heading: III. CLOCK ENERGY INJECTION
sections.text:
As the previous section shows, the capacitive energy harvester uses a source-referenced clock to drive the MOSFET. Typically, this gate drive is undesirable because the floating reference voltage makes implementation difficult. Here, SPICE simulation explains the necessity of this choice. Table I shows simulated data when the clock is referenced to ground. Circuit parameters used in the simulation are $\mathrm { C _ { R E S } = }$ F, $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } } = 3 . 3 \ : \mathrm { n F }$ , $R _ { \mathrm { L O A D } } = 2 0 \mathrm { M } \Omega , L _ { \mathrm { F L Y } } = 2 . 5 \mathrm { m H }$ , $R _ { \mathrm { C O R E } } ~ = ~ 3 6 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , $R _ { \mathrm { W I R E } } ~ = ~ 8 ~ \Omega$ , $v _ { \mathrm { t h } } = 2 . 5 \ : \mathrm { V }$ , ${ \mathit { C } } _ { \mathrm { { D C } } } =$ $1 . 2 2 \mathrm { n F }$ , $C _ { \mathrm { A C } } = 3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { p F }$ , $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } } = 6 \ : \mathrm { V }$ , $f _ { \mathrm { C L K } } = 4 7 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , and $D = 0 . 0 0 1 9$ . The simulation uses a SPICE Level-3 2N7002 $\mathbf { n }$ -channel MOSFET model and a realistic diode model based on the characteristics of a 1N6263 low-leakage Schottky barrier diode. In the table, $v _ { \mathrm { R E S , 0 } }$ and $v _ { \mathrm { R E S , \infty } }$ represent the original and final voltages on $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ , respectively. Furthermore, $v _ { G }$ is the magnitude of the gate drive voltage. In all cases, $v _ { G }$ exceeds the MOSFET threshold voltage, so the on-resistance of the MOSFET does not change much between simulations. The important point to observe is that the converted power $P _ { \mathrm { C O N V } }$ rises significantly as $v _ { G }$ increases. Given that all other parameters remain fixed, the additional harvested energy must come from the clock. This is important for two reasons. First, in an experimental system in which the MOSFET is not powered by $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ , energy injection from the clock through the MOSFET gate can be confused as net energy conversion when in fact net energy is not converted. Second, the energy injected into the harvester diminishes the energy that can actually be harvested during a cycle. To understand the source of clock energy injection, consider the simplified circuit diagram shown in Fig. 5. In this figure, $C _ { \mathrm { G S } }$ is the MOSFET gate-source capacitance, $D _ { 3 }$ is the MOSFET body diode, and $C _ { 1 }$ is the parasitic junction capacitance of $D _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ . When a rising clock places $Q _ { \mathrm { G S } }$ onto $C _ { \mathrm { G S } }$ , the voltage at node X rises according to the capacitive divider involving $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { \mathrm { G S } }$ . If the voltage rises enough, $D _ { 3 }$ turns on and leaks a fraction of $Q _ { \mathrm { G S } }$ onto $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ , which cannot be recovered when the clock goes low. Using a source-referenced clock prevents node X from being pulled up, thereby preventing the accidental turn-on of $D _ { 3 }$ and the corresponding energy injection. sections.heading: IV. VARIABLE CAPACITOR
sections.text:
To test the asynchronous capacitive energy harvesting circuit, a macro scale spring steel variable capacitor supported by eight cantilever beams was designed and fabricated. As shown in Figs. 6 and 7, a square sheet of $0 . 0 5 ^ { \prime \prime }$ thick 1095 blue-tempered spring steel, with a mass density of $7 8 5 0 \mathrm { k g / m ^ { 3 } }$ and a Young’s Modulus of $2 0 5 \mathrm { G P a }$ , measuring $6 . 6 ~ \mathrm { c m }$ on each side formed the flexible top plate of $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ . A solid block of aluminum formed the base. Mylar tape acted as a spacer that defined the nominal gap between the plates. To prevent the top and bottom plates from shorting, nylon screws were used to hold the structure together. FEA optimization was used to keep the out-of-plane resonant mode close to $1 5 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ while pushing the torsion and rotation modes toward higher frequencies above $6 0 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . The resulting springs have lengths of $0 . 8 ~ \mathrm { c m }$ and widths of $0 . 7 \mathrm { c m }$ . Finally, fillets with $2 \mathrm { m m }$ radii were inserted at all perpendicular intersections to help reduce stress levels in the bending capacitor plate.

The prototype spring steel variable capacitor gave ${ \it C } _ { \mathrm { d c } } =$ $6 5 0 ~ \mathrm { p F }$ when measured on a standard bridge, which is close to the calculated value of ${ 5 6 6 } \ \mathrm { p F } .$ . The capacitor was vibrated with a Ling Dynamic System V456 shaker table and its corresponding PA $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { L }$ amplifier. Using the circuit shown in Fig. 8, in which $v _ { \mathrm { T E S T } }$ is proportional to $C _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ , a frequency sweep was performed. The result in Fig. 8 shows the first resonant mode to be at $f = 1 5 6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ with a $Q$ of approximately 3.5. Next, by applying $1 5 6 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ vibrations of varying strengths to the variable capacitor, created by changing the peak-to-peak voltage input $ { v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p - p } }$ to the PA 1000L amplifier, a plot of $C _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ as a function of $ { v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p - p } }$ was generated. Fig. 9 shows the collected data.

sections.heading: V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.text:
The circuit in Fig. 2 was fabricated using surface mount components to test the validity of SPICE simulation results and to demonstrate its operation. The components include a 2N7002 n-channel MOSFET, three 1N6263 low-leakage Schottky barrier diodes, and a CD4047 low power monostable multivibrator gate drive. Before every experiment, a shorting jumper connects a battery to precharge $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ up to $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } } = 1 . 5 \ : \mathrm { V }$ , the starting steady-state voltage. The shaker table is then ramped up from no shaking to the desired test level and the jumper is disconnected. In all cases, the flyback circuit is activated after every 4 energy conversion cycles.

Because a resistive load $R _ { \mathrm { L O A D } }$ formed by a $1 0 \mathbf { M } \boldsymbol { \Omega }$ scope probe in series with a $1 0 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ resistor is attached to the reservoir, a rising $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ indicates positive energy conversion. Fig. 10 plots the evolution of $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ for various shaker table amplifier inputs $ { v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p - p } }$ . When $v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p - p } = 1 2 0 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ $\mathit { C _ { A C } } = 8 4 \ : \mathrm { p F } ,$ , the energy harvester just barely sustains $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ while powering the

$2 0 { \bf M } \Omega$ load. For $v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p \mathrm { - } p } = 3 6 0 ~ \mathrm { m V } ( C _ { \mathrm { A C } } = 2 6 0 ~ \mathrm { p F } )$ , $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ charges up to $6 \mathrm { V } ,$ which means that the system delivers $1 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ to $R _ { \mathrm { L O A D } }$ .

Although the energy harvester does not have an integrated acceleration sensor to determine the applied acceleration directly, an approximate value can be obtained at the resonant frequency. Assuming a sinusoidal travel of the upper variable capacitor plate and using $Q \approx 3 . 5$ from Fig. 8, and the nominal dimensions of the variable capacitor, the applied acceleration per 100 $\mathrm { m V }$ of $v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p - p }$ is approximately $8 . 4 ~ \mathrm { g }$ where $g = 9 . { \overset { \cdot } { 8 } } \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . This translates to $4 0 \ \mathrm { g }$ when $C _ { \mathrm { A C } } = 3 5 0 { \mathrm { p F } }$ .

Notice that the plots in Fig. 10 all flatten out and saturate. This is due to the nonlinear core loss present in $L _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ that increases as $v _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ goes up. In Fig. 2, this nonlinearity is modeled as a nonlinear resistor $R _ { \mathrm { C O R E } }$ whose resistance depends on $v _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ As $v _ { \mathrm { F L Y } }$ varies between $_ { 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } }$ and $3 \ \mathrm { V } ,$ , $R _ { \mathrm { C O R E } }$ drops from its nominal value of $4 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ down to approximately $1 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .

To prove that the harvested energy does not include clock energy injection, two additional experiments are performed. First, the shaker table is stopped while the clock signal continued running. The scope probe attached to $C _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ shows that $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ decays to below $8 0 ~ \mathrm { m V } ,$ , much lower than the voltages sustained in Fig. 10. This strongly suggests that even if there is energy injection from the source-referenced clock, it is small compared to the transduced energy. Next, the MOSFET clock amplitude, or equivalently $v _ { \mathrm { G S } }$ , is varied to determined its effect on the harvested energy. The result, shown in Fig. 11, indicates that the amount of harvested energy is independent of $v _ { \mathrm { G S } }$ , consistent with SPICE simulations presented in Table II. Thus, it is believed that no energy injected through the MOSFET gate is present in Fig. 10.

If the capacitive energy harvester is to be integrated onto an IC with a MEMS capacitor, the minimum $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ required for system startup is critical. A high requirement would necessitate electrochemical cells, defeating the purpose of using an energy harvester in the first place. Startup tests were conducted for the prototype circuit by lowering $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ using a voltage divider and observing whether $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ could still rise to the levels shown in Fig. 10. Fig. 12 plots a sample result with $v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p - p } = 3 2 0 \mathrm { m V }$ and $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } } = 2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ at the start. An iteration process shows that even at the noise floor of the oscilloscope, around $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } } =$ $8 9 \mathrm { m V }$ , the system can still startup, allowing for a piezoelectric film or an electret to jump start the harvester.

![](images/9bfc29bc320ceb97f457a017c2f93db81662b97dfd2210292438adbd3303844e.jpg)  
Fig. 11. $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ as a function of source-referenced clocking voltage.

![](images/420c428388090a653b51ce43cf4a3a0501c8b93a66aea95222756299751454c5.jpg)  
Fig. 12. Plot of $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ as circuit starts up from $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } } ~ = ~ 2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ when $v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p ^ { - } p } = 3 2 0 \ \mathrm { m V }$ .

![](images/b236cfadedcccde1fa2e3e38c30e367201b8268db2e3e810601a9d914b861858.jpg)  
Fig. 13. Plot of saturation $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ as a function of frequency with $v _ { \mathrm { A M P } , p - p } =$ $3 2 0 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ .

In real world applications, the vibration frequency will have some spread, so the sensitivity of the capacitive energy harvester to frequency variations is also important. Fig. 13 shows the saturation point of $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ as a function of the drive frequency at - mV. From this plot, a deviation of 150 Hz from the resonant frequency causes a $37 \%$ drop in the saturation voltage, which may be unacceptable. A reduction in the mechanical $Q$ will lower this sensitivity at the cost of $C _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ , so a tradeoff exists. If the frequency spectrum of the ambient vibration is not known a priori, the variable capacitor can be designed with a tunable resonant frequency, perhaps through an adaptive scheme employing electric spring stiffening.

sections.heading: VI. ENERGY CONVERSION EFFICIENCY
sections.text:
Having demonstrated the behavior of the capacitive energy harvester, the energy conversion efficiency of the circuit is now computed. As a figure of merit, the efficiency $\eta$ will be defined as

$$
\eta \equiv \frac { \mathrm { P o w e r ~ d e l i v e r e d ~ t o ~ l o a d } } { \mathrm { T h e o r e t i c a l ~ p o w e r ~ h a r v e s t e d ~ f r o m } Q \lnot V \mathrm { c y c l e } } .
$$

The numerator represents the amount of useful energy the harvester can provide to a load while the denominator represents the theoretical maximum that the circuit can deliver if the process was $100 \%$ efficient.

As mentioned in Section V, the prototype system presents $6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ to a $2 0 { \mathrm { ~ M } } \Omega$ resistive load under heavy shaking. Hence, the amount of power delivered to the load for that experiment is $1 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ . To determine the denominator, we can compute the total enclosed area $A _ { 1 } + A _ { 2 }$ in Fig. 4. For simplicity, approximate $A _ { 2 }$ as a triangle. Also, because the flyback switch is enabled every 4 harvesting cycles in this paper, take $n = 2$ in (8) to find the average energy harvested per cycle. Begin by considering Point 1, which corresponds to the moment when both $D _ { 1 }$ and $D _ { 2 }$ are off and the plates of the variable capacitor are beginning to pull apart. At this point,

$$
v _ { 1 } = V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } = 6 \ V
$$

and therefore

$$
Q _ { 1 } = Q _ { 2 } = C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } = 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { C } .
$$

Point 2 occurs when $D _ { 2 }$ turns on, and this happens when $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ is equal to the previous cycle’s , which is just $v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } , 1 }$ . From (8) with $n = 1$ , $v _ { \mathrm { S T O R E , 1 } } = 7 . 2 ~ \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , so $v _ { 2 } = 7 . 2 ~ \mathrm { V }$ . The trace between Points 2 and 3 represents the charge transfer between $C _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ and $C _ { \mathrm { S T O R E } }$ when $D _ { 2 }$ turns on. By setting $n =$ in (8), it is obtained that $v _ { 3 } = 8 . 2 \ : \mathrm { V }$ . From this, one can also calculate that

$$
Q _ { 3 } = Q _ { 4 } = C _ { \mathrm { M I N } } v _ { 3 } = 2 . 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { C } .
$$

Finally, the capacitor plates move toward each other until $D _ { 1 }$ turns on, from which point on $v _ { \mathrm { V A R } }$ is held at $V _ { \mathrm { R E S } }$ until the end of the cycle. Therefore,

$$
\begin{array} { r } { v _ { 4 } = V _ { \mathrm { R E S } } = 6 \mathbf { V } . } \end{array}
$$

Having determined all the necessary values, areas $A _ { 1 }$ and $A _ { 2 }$ can be computed as

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { A _ { 1 } = ( v _ { 2 } - v _ { 1 } ) ( Q _ { 1 } - Q _ { 4 } ) = 4 . 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { ~ J } } } \\ { { A _ { 2 } = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( v _ { 3 } - v _ { 2 } ) ( Q _ { 1 } - Q _ { 4 } ) = 1 . 8 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { ~ J } . } } \end{array}
$$

Therefore, the average converted energy $W _ { \mathrm { C O N V } }$ per cycle is

$$
W _ { \mathrm { C O N V } } = A _ { 1 } + A _ { 2 } = 6 \mathrm { n J }
$$

which means that

$$
P _ { \mathrm { C O N V } } = W _ { \mathrm { C O N V } } f = 9 . 4 \mu \mathrm { W } .
$$

Finally, referring back to (13),

$$
\eta = \frac { 1 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W } } { 9 . 4 \mu \mathrm { W } } = 1 9 . 1 \% .
$$

An efficiency that removes the losses of the MOSFET and diodes can also be calculated. This value corresponds to the deliverable power given lossless power electronics. Because the MOSFET on-resistance, $R _ { \mathrm { D S , O N } }$ , is approximately a constant when operated as a switch, the average conduction loss, $\langle P _ { \mathrm { F E T , C O N D } } \rangle$ , is related to the root-mean-square current, $i _ { \mathrm { R M S } }$ . Using typical parameter values from the 2N7002 n-channel MOSFET datasheet,

$$
\langle P _ { \mathrm { F E T , C O N D } } \rangle \approx i _ { \mathrm { R M S } } ^ { 2 } \times R _ { \mathrm { D S , O N } } = 0 . 3 6 ~ \mathrm { n W } .
$$

The value of $i _ { \mathrm { R M S } } = 1 4 \mu \mathrm { A }$ comes from HSPICE simulation [10]. On the other hand, diodes have a constant voltage drop, $v _ { D }$ , across them when turned on, so their average conduction loss is related to the average current, $\langle i _ { D } \rangle$ . Using typical parameter values from the 1N6263 Schottky diode datasheet,

$$
\langle P _ { D , \mathrm { C O N D } } \rangle \approx \langle i _ { D } \rangle v _ { D } = 2 \mu \mathrm { W } .
$$

Again, the value of $\langle i _ { D } \rangle = 1 0 \mu \mathrm { A }$ comes from HSPICE simulation [10]. Adding these losses to the numerator, one obtains

$$
\eta ^ { \prime } = \frac { 3 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W } } { 9 . 4 \mu \mathrm { W } } = 4 0 . 4 \% .
$$

sections.heading: VII. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION
sections.text: This paper demonstrates an asynchronous capacitive energy harvesting circuit employing a charge pump and inductive flyback. Coupled to an experimental variable capacitor, it delivers $1 . 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ of power to a $2 0 { \mathrm { ~ M } } \Omega$ resistive load at a steady-state voltage of $6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ while exhibiting an efficiency of $1 9 . 1 \%$ . The spring steel variable capacitor used to drive the charge pump achieved a $C _ { \mathrm { M A X } } / C _ { \mathrm { M I N } }$ ratio of 3.3 with a $1 . 5 6 \mathrm { ~ k H z }$ out-ofplane resonant frequency. Because the harvester employs only one asynchronous MOSFET switch, clocking is greatly simplified. However, this paper shows that in order to obtain accurate data, a source-referenced gate drive should be used to prevent spurious clock energy injection, which can artificially inflate the conversion efficiency and diminish actual conversion. Experiments conducted using a prototype circuit not only demonstrated close match between theory and actual data, but they also revealed an extremely low startup requirement of $v _ { \mathrm { R E S } } \leq$ $8 9 \mathrm { m V }$ for the capacitive harvester. Finally, the system can tolerate a frequency variation of $1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ before the steady-state voltage drops to 2/3 of its peak value.
